system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 19 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2186-05-22 08:26:00 to 2186-06-09 13:57:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 54-year-old woman with a history of Crohn’s disease, short bowel syndrome, and prior venous thrombosis was admitted for worsening abdominal pain, distention, and vomiting. Imaging showed bowel distention consistent with paralytic ileus rather than mechanical obstruction, with a known colonic stricture unchanged from prior studies. She was managed conservatively with bowel rest, an NG tube, IV fluids, and IV hydromorphone for pain. Ciprofloxacin and metronidazole were continued for a presumed Crohn’s flare, and fondaparinux was maintained for prior upper extremity DVT. Her pain was partially complicated by PTSD, which was managed with diazepam and supportive care. The NG tube was removed after she tolerated oral intake, and pain control was transitioned to oral hydromorphone. She improved over nine days, was discharged home on oral medications, and scheduled for outpatient GI follow-up.
problems: Phlebitis and thrombophlebitis of upper extremities, unspecified
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism

___ y/o female with a PMH of Crohn's disease s/p multiple 
resections and repeated episodes of obstruction who presented to

pain, abdominal distention, and 1 day of NBNB vomiting 
transferred from MICU to ___ 2 on HD 2 in stable condition with

known Crohn's and s/p multiple resections with a history of 
recurrent partial obstructions; presentation was similar to 
previous episodes with the exception of new chills, fever to 101 
and gap acidosis - the latter resolved the second day of 
admission. Started on Cipro/Flagyl for a presumed Crohn's flare 
with possible bacterial translocation into the abdomen and 
subsequently defervesced. Underwent colonoscopy and balloon 
dilation as detailed above. Subsequent to colonscopy and the

bowel rest and intermittent NGT suction. Rifaxamin was started

dilaudid titrated to effect in conjunction with valium in the

medications were downtitrated and transitioned to PO as 
permitted by negotiations with the patient. Diet was advanced as 
tolerated. Discharged in stable condition with no significant 
abdominal pain, no nausea, and tolerating a full diet. In 
addition to the diazepam detailed below, was also discharged 
with a 14 day prescription of PO dilaudid with an oral agreement 
made to follow-up with Dr. ___ days after discharge to 
assess her pain regimen.
.  
# Crohn's Disease: Presumed to be the primary etiology of the 
patient's presentation. Dr. ___ team consulted and 
recommended continuing Cipro/Flagyl until the patient was 
asymptomatic in addition to the diet and pain management as 
detailed above; she was also treated with a course of Rifaximin 
for bacterial overgrowth and was discharged on this medication. 
The patient was discharged with close follow-up with Dr. ___ 
and with her PCP.
.

diazepam weaned over the course of the hospitalization and 
discharged with 14 days of diazepam with an oral agreement that 
she was to self-downtitrate and follow-up with her PCP regarding 
whether to continue this medication in 2 weeks.
.
# Iron deficiency anemia: Treated with IV iron dextran and 
ferric gluconate as an inpatient.
.
# Acute renal insufficiency: Creatinine normalized from 1.1 on 
admission to baseline 0.6 with PO hydration.

# RUE extremity swelling: Pt w/ Chronic narrowing of the SVC, 
including a focal segment of wall thickening/chronic thrombus 
along its anterior margin. DVT was ruled out with RU dopplers 
and swelling resolved after one day with warm compresses and 
elevation.

hospitalization on home synthroid.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ y/o female with a PMH of Crohn's disease s/p multiple 
resections and repeated episodes of obstruction who presented to 
the ED with 1 day of progressively worsening lower abdominal 
pain, abdominal distention, and 1 day of NBNB vomiting 
transferred from MICU to ___ 2 on HD 2 in stable condition with 
multiple days of nausea bloating and pain despite NGT/NPO in the 
setting of an abscence of objective obstructive findings.
.
A detailed problem list is as follows:
.
# Abdominal pain, fever, chills: Pain was in the setting of 
known Crohn's and s/p multiple resections with a history of 
recurrent partial obstructions; presentation was similar to 
previous episodes with the exception of new chills, fever to 101 
and gap acidosis - the latter resolved the second day of 
admission. Started on Cipro/Flagyl for a presumed Crohn's flare 
with possible bacterial translocation into the abdomen and 
subsequently defervesced. Underwent colonoscopy and balloon 
dilation as detailed above. Subsequent to colonscopy and the 
initiation of antibiotics, symptoms gradually improved with 
bowel rest and intermittent NGT suction. Rifaxamin was started 
per GI for bacterial overgrowth. Pain was managed with IV 
dilaudid titrated to effect in conjunction with valium in the 
acute setting; as her clinical status stabilized, these 
medications were downtitrated and transitioned to PO as 
permitted by negotiations with the patient. Diet was advanced as 
tolerated. Discharged in stable condition with no significant 
abdominal pain, no nausea, and tolerating a full diet. In 
addition to the diazepam detailed below, was also discharged 
with a 14 day prescription of PO dilaudid with an oral agreement 
made to follow-up with Dr. ___ days after discharge to 
assess her pain regimen.
.  
# Crohn's Disease: Presumed to be the primary etiology of the 
patient's presentation. Dr. ___ team consulted and 
recommended continuing Cipro/Flagyl until the patient was 
asymptomatic in addition to the diet and pain management as 
detailed above; she was also treated with a course of Rifaximin 
for bacterial overgrowth and was discharged on this medication. 
The patient was discharged with close follow-up with Dr. ___ 
and with her PCP.
.
# PTSD/Depression/Anxiety: Continued home citalopram. IV 
diazepam weaned over the course of the hospitalization and 
discharged with 14 days of diazepam with an oral agreement that 
she was to self-downtitrate and follow-up with her PCP regarding 
whether to continue this medication in 2 weeks.
.
# Iron deficiency anemia: Treated with IV iron dextran and 
ferric gluconate as an inpatient.
.
# Acute renal insufficiency: Creatinine normalized from 1.1 on 
admission to baseline 0.6 with PO hydration.
.  
# RUE extremity swelling: Pt w/ Chronic narrowing of the SVC, 
including a focal segment of wall thickening/chronic thrombus 
along its anterior margin. DVT was ruled out with RU dopplers 
and swelling resolved after one day with warm compresses and 
elevation.
.  
# Hypothyroidism: Clinically euthyroid during the 
hospitalization on home synthroid.
.
Remained full code for the duration of the hospitalization.

INDICATION:  ___ woman with Crohn's disease, status post multiple
resections and small bowel obstructions, presents with pain, distention,
rigors.

TECHNIQUE:  Contiguous MDCT images through the abdomen and pelvis were
performed after administration of oral contrast.  Axial, coronal and sagittal
reformats were acquired.

COMPARISON:  CT of the abdomen and pelvis from ___.

FINDINGS:

CT OF THE ABDOMEN:  

There is minimal basilar atelectasis at the right lung.  

Assessment of solid visceral structures is limited without intravenous
contrast.  Allowing for this, the liver is normal.  There is no intra- or
extra-hepatic biliary dilatation.  The pancreas, spleen, both adrenal glands
and kidneys are normal. Gallbladder is nonvisualized.

There are multiple scattered non-pathologically enlarged retroperitoneal lymph
nodes.  Redemonstrated are multiple mesenteric lymph nodes, predominantly at
the right lower quadrant measuring up to 9 mm, unchanged.
There are no significant atherosclerotic calcifications of the abdominal
arterial system.

There is no free air and no free fluid.

The small bowel is filled with contrast without evidence of bowel wall
thickening or small bowel obstruction.  The patient had multiple prior both
small and large bowel resections with a neoterminal ileum in the right mid
abdomen.  There is unchanged mild dilatation of the neoterminal ileum proximal
to the anastomosis site (series 2, image 41) and mild large bowel wall
thickening and narrowing distal to the anastomosis site (series 2, image 43),
unchanged from prior exam and likely representing a fixed stenosis and chronic
postinflammatory change.

CT OF THE PELVIS: 

The large bowel is air filled and slightly dilated.  There are multiple new
areas of bowel wall thickening and narrowing in between areas of mildly
dilated large bowel loops, predominantly at the sigmoid colon (series 2, image
64, series 2, image 70 and series 2, image 70). However, this most likely
represents bowel peristalis as these were not present in the study of
___, and are thus less likely skip lesions from Crohn disease.

There is no free fluid in the pelvis.  The urinary bladder, vagina are normal.
There are no pelvic hernias.

BONES:  

There are bilateral chronic sacroiliitis.  No evidence of suspicious lytic or
sclerotic bony lesions.  There are calcified granulomas in the soft tissues
overlying large gluteal muscles likely from prior subcutaneous injections.

IMPRESSION:

1.  No evidence of small or large bowel obstruction.

2.  Multiple areas of large bowel wall pseudo-thickening and narrowing, new
compared to prior, likely represents peristalsis, less likely consistent skip
lesions; however, evaluation is limited without oral and IV contrast.

3.  Unchanged fixed narrowing of large bowel distal to the anastomosis site
with the neoterminal ileum with mild dilatation of the neoterminal ileum.

___ is the attending radiologist and was supervising throughout.

ANESTHESIA:  A 1% lidocaine.  Moderate sedation was provided by administering
divided doses of fentanyl and Versed throughout the total intraservice time of
25 minutes during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were continuously
monitored.  In total, the patient received 50 mcg of fentanyl and 1 mg of
Versed.

PROCEDURE AND FINDINGS:  Written informed consent was obtained prior to the
procedure with the indication, alternatives, risks and benefits explained. 
The patient demonstrated good understanding of these features.  The patient
was brought to the angiography suite and placed supine on the imaging table.
The right side of the neck was prepped and draped in the typical sterile
fashion.  A preprocedure timeout was performed using name, date of birth and
medical record number as identifiers.

Under sonographic guidance, the right internal jugular vein was accessed with
a micropuncture set and images were saved to PACS.  A 0.035 ___ wire was
placed through the micropuncture sheath and advanced into the inferior vena
cava under fluoroscopic guidance after taking appropriate measurements. 
Micropuncture sheath was removed and the soft tissue tract was dilated.  A 7
___, 16 cm temporary triple-lumen central venous catheter was placed over
the Guidewire and the Guidewire was removed.  All three ports of the catheter
were aspirated and flushed easily.  Catheter was secured to the skin with 0
silk sutures and a sterile dressing was applied.  A fluoroscopic chest film
was obtained demonstrating satisfactory placement of the catheter with the tip
terminating in the distal SVC.  The patient tolerated the procedure well and
there were no immediate complications.

IMPRESSION:  Successful placement of a temporary triple-lumen right internal
jugular central venous catheter with the tip terminating in the distal SVC.
The line is ready for use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You came in last night with abdominal pain, fever, and shaking. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I woke up around 1 a.m. with a fever—up to 101—and then started shivering badly by 2 a.m. My left lower belly pain came back, worse than before, and I vomited twice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And does this pain feel like your previous episodes of bowel obstruction?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly the same. I’ve been more bloated lately too. I haven’t had a bowel movement in a day, but I am passing gas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The CT scan shows no bowel obstruction, but there’s a known narrowing at your ileal-colonic connection, and some new areas of thickening that may just be muscle spasms. We’re treating this as a Crohn’s flare with possible infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not another blockage? But why the fever and shaking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think the inflammation from Crohn’s may have let bacteria into the area, causing the fever. We’ve started antibiotics—Flagyl, ceftriaxone, and Levaquin—to cover that possibility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had an NG tube placed last night. Is that still needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for now. It’s helping to decompress your stomach since you’re nauseous and distended. We’ll check X-rays to make sure it’s in the right place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The chest X-ray shows your NG tube was too high earlier, but we’ve adjusted it. It’s now sitting in your stomach, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense—I felt like it wasn’t helping at first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re concerned about your IV access because of your history. We’re going to place a central line in your neck so we can give antibiotics and fluids safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had trouble with lines before. Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll use ultrasound to guide it, and you’ll get light sedation. It’s the best way to ensure we can deliver your meds reliably.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The central line was placed yesterday. How are you feeling? Still in pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still bloated and sore. The pain meds help a little, but I’m anxious too—being in the hospital brings back bad memories.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve continued your citalopram and are using diazepam when needed for anxiety. We’ll keep the environment calm and give you space when you need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures came back negative—no bloodstream infection. Stool tests also ruled out C. diff and other pathogens. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s definitely Crohn’s then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely. But we still need to check the narrowing in your bowel. We’re planning a colonoscopy tomorrow with possible dilation if it’s tight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that hurt? I’m nervous about the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be under moderate sedation—fentanyl and Versed—so you’ll be very relaxed and won’t feel much. We’ll monitor you closely the whole time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You had the colonoscopy this morning. We found inflammation and narrowing at the anastomosis site. We took biopsies and dilated the stricture with a balloon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did it go well? Was there bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it went smoothly. There was a small amount of bleeding after dilation, but it stopped on its own. The biopsies will confirm the extent of inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the biopsies—how long to get results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A few days. But based on what we saw, it looks like active Crohn’s inflammation, especially at the connection site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your white count has improved, and your kidney function is recovering. Your creatinine was 1.1 on admission but is now 0.5—great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been so dehydrated before. I’m glad that’s better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re giving you fluids by mouth now, which is helping. We’re also starting rifaximin for bacterial overgrowth, which can worsen bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My right arm is swelling up. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re checking it. You have a history of SVC narrowing, so we’re doing an ultrasound to rule out a clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the ultrasound showed no acute clot. The swelling is likely due to your chronic vein narrowing. We’ll use warm compresses and elevation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s already feeling a bit better. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to try advancing your diet today—starting with clear liquids. How’s your nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I think I can try some broth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well on liquids. We’re removing the NG tube today since you’re not vomiting and your belly is less distended.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I hated that tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The biopsy results are back. They show chronic active inflammation at the anastomosis with gastric metaplasia—consistent with Crohn’s. There’s also mild colitis higher up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s still active, even with my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, which is why you had this flare. We’ll continue the antibiotics and rifaximin, and your GI doctor wants you to follow up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re now on a full soft diet and walking regularly. Your pain is much better—we’re switching from IV to oral Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I was worried about staying on IV meds too long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also started IV iron for your anemia. You’ve been deficient for a while, and this will help your energy and healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been so tired. I hope this helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest X-ray shows persistent but stable bowel dilation. No free air, which means no perforation. You’re healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my breathing? I’ve noticed some spots on my chest X-rays.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The patchy areas are chronic—likely old inflammation or bronchiectasis. No pneumonia or new fluid. Your lungs are clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had some increased nausea last night. The X-ray showed slightly worse bowel dilation, but we think it’s due to temporary slowing. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt bloated again. But I’m not vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll hold off on the NG tube for now. Just rest your bowel for a few hours and we’ll try liquids again later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—you’re improving again. The last X-ray shows no free air and stable findings. We’re confident you’re on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you keep tolerating food and staying pain-free, likely in the next two days. We’ll finalize your discharge plan tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. You’re off IV meds, eating regular food, and your labs are stable. We’re planning discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds will I go home on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue cipro, metronidazole, and now add rifaximin. We’re giving you a 14-day supply of oral Dilaudid and Valium for pain and anxiety, to taper as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your GI doctor in two weeks. Also follow up with your PCP about the Valium taper and your iron levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re discharged. Keep taking your meds, rest, and call if you develop fever, severe pain, or can’t keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your discharge instructions include stopping oxazepam and metaxalone. They’re not needed anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll make sure to update my list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep using the lidocaine patch for any localized pain. It’s safe with your other meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve found it helpful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Someone will bring your prescriptions and discharge papers shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home and rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. Enjoy being home, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also send a summary to your PCP and GI doctor so they’re up to date.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep taking your levothyroxine and citalopram as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t missed those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Stay consistent. You’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we ask. Take it one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 54-year-old woman with a history of Crohn’s disease, short bowel syndrome, and multiple prior surgeries was admitted for fever, rigors, and worsening left lower quadrant abdominal pain with distention and vomiting. Imaging showed no mechanical obstruction but revealed a fixed stricture at the ileocolonic anastomosis and new areas of bowel wall thickening likely due to peristalsis. She was treated for a presumed Crohn’s flare with antibiotics (ciprofloxacin, metronidazole, and later rifaximin), bowel rest, and NG tube decompression. A colonoscopy confirmed active inflammation and stricture, which was dilated. IV iron was given for iron deficiency anemia, and her acute kidney injury resolved with hydration. Her PTSD and anxiety were managed with diazepam, which was transitioned to oral taper. She gradually improved, tolerated a full diet, and was discharged home on oral medications with follow-up plans.
